name: Antiphilus of Byzantium
bio: Antiphilus of Byzantium wrote in the first century AD and is one of the poets of the Garland of Philippus. His epigrams include love poems, dedications and little pictures of daily life.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poems.title: Book V, 111
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I sang even formerly, when Tereina’s charms were yet infantile, “She will consume us all when she grows up.” They laughed at my prophecy: but lo! the time I once foretold is come, and for long I suffer myself from the wound. What am I to do? To look on her is pure fire, and to look away is trouble of heart, and if I pay my suit to her, it is “I ama maid.”’ All is over with me.

poems.title: Book V, 307: On a Picture of Zeus and Leda
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: This is the Laconian river Eurotas, and that is Leda with nothing on, and he who is hidden in the swan is Zeus. And you little Cupids, who are luring me so little disposed to love, what bird am I to become? If Zeus is a swan, I suppose I must be lark.

poems.title: Book VI, 95
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Paris the husbandman, resting from his sore toil, dedicates to Demeter his ox-turning iron-tipped, threatening goad, his bag, measure of the seedcorn, his curved sickle, husbandry’s weapon, that cuts off the corn-ears, his winnowing fork, three-fingered hand of the harvest, that throws the corn up against the wind, and his laced boots.

poems.title: Book VI, 97
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: The spear of Alexander; the inscription on thee tells that after the war he dedicated thee to Artemis as a token thereof, the weapon of his invincible arm. O good spear, before the shaking of which earth and sea yielded! Hail, fearless spear! and ever all who look on thee will tremble, mindful of that mighty hand.

poems.title: Book VI, 199
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Artemis, goddess of the road, Antiphilus dedicates to thee this hat from his head, a token of his wayfaring; for thou hast hearkened to his vows, thou hast blessed his paths. The gift is not great, but given in piety, and let no covetous traveller lay his hand on my offering; it is not safe to despoil a shrine of even little gifts.

poems.title: Book VI, 250
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: My circumstances are slender, madam, but I maintain that he who is yours from his heart looks down on the wealth of many. But accept this garment like the bright purple of a deep-piled carpet soft as moss, and this pink wool, and spikenard for your dark hair contained in a gray glass bottle, so that the tunic may cover you, the woollen work may testify to the skill of your hands, and the sweet vapour may pervade your hair.

poems.title: Book VI, 252
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I am a quince of last year kept fresh in my young skin, unspotted, unwrinkled, as downy as newly-born ones, still attached to my leafy stalk, a rare gift in the winter season ; but for such as thou, my queen, even the cold and snow bear fruit.

poems.title: Book VI, 257
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Who filled me with the gifts of Demeter, the amphora fashioned for Bacchus, the recipient of Adriatic wine sweet as nectar? Why should he grudge me to Bacchus, or what scarcity was there of proper vessels for corn? He insulted both divinities ; Bacchus has been robbed, and Demeter does not receive Methé I into her society.

poems.title: Book VII, 141: On Protesilaus
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: O Thessalian Protesilaus, long ages shall sing of thee, how thou didst strike the first blow in Troy’s predestined fall. The Nymphs tend and encircle with overshadowing elms thy tomb opposite hated Ilion. Wrathful are the trees, and if they chance to see the walls of Troy, they shed their withered leaves. How bitter was the hatred of the heroes if a part of their enmity lives yet in soulless branches.

poems.title: Book VII, 175
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: So there is no more turf, husbandman, left for thee to break up, and thy oxen tread on the backs of tombs, and the share is among the dead! What doth it profit thee? How much is this wheat ye shall snatch from ashes, not from earth? Ye shall not live for ever, and another shall plough you up, you who set to all the example of this evil husbandry.

poems.title: Book VII, 176
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Nor because I lacked funeral when I died, do I lie here, a naked corpse on wheat-bearing land. Duly was I buried once on a time, but now by the ploughman’s hand the iron share hath rolled me out of my tomb. Who said that death was deliverance from evil, when not even the tomb, stranger, is the end of my sufferings?

poems.title: Book VII, 375: Not Sepulchral
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: My house collapsed with the earthquake; yet my chamber remained erect, as its walls stood the shock. There while I lay, as if hiding in a cave, the unhappy labour-pains overtook me, and another dread was mingled with that of the earthquake. Nature herself was the midwife, and the child and I both together saw the sun above the earth.

poems.title: Book VII, 379: Not Sepulchral
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: A, “Tell me, Dicaearchia, why thou hast built thee so vast a mole in the sea, reaching out to the middle of the deep? They were Cyclopes’ hands that planted such walls in the sea. How long, O Land, shalt thou do violence to us?” B. “I can receive the navies of the world. Look at Rome hard by; is not my harbour as great as she?”

poems.title: Book VII, 399
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Far from each other should the tombs of Oedipus’ sons have been built, for even Hades ends not their strife. They refused even to travel in one boat to the house of Acheron, and hateful Ares lives in them even now they are dead. Look at the uneven flame of their pyre, how it separates from one into two quarrelling tongues.

poems.title: Book VII, 622
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: When Borchus the neat-herd went to get the sweet honey-comb, climbing the steep rock by a rope, one of his dogs who used to follow the herd followed him, and, as he was pulling himself up, bit through the thin rope which was trickling with honey. He fell into Hades, grasping, at the cost of his life, that honey which no other man could harvest.

poems.title: Book VII, 630
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Now nearing my country I said, “To-morrow shall this wind that blew so long against me abate.” Scarce had I closed my lips when the sea became like hell, and that light word I spoke was my destruction. Beware ever of that word to-morrow ”; not even little things are unnoticed by the Nemesis that is the foe of our tongues.

poems.title: Book VII, 634
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Old Philo, stooping to lift the bier to gain his daily wage, stumbled slightly, but fell and was killed; for he was ripe for Hades, and old age was on the look out for an opportunity; and so all unawares he lifted for himself that bier on which he used to carry the corpses of others.

poems.title: Book VII, 635
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Hierocles’ boat grew old with him, always travelled with him, and accompanied him in life and in death. It was his faithful fishing partner, and no juster boat ever sailed the waves. It laboured to keep him until his old age, and then it buried him when he was dead, and travelled with him to Hades.

poems.title: Book VII, 641: Not Sepulchral, but on a Water-clock
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: This recorder of the invisible sun, divided into twelve parts, and as often speaking with tongueless mouth, each time that, the water being compressed in the narrow pipe, the air sends forth a sonorous blast, was erected by Athenaeus for the public, so that the sun might be visible even when covered by envious clouds.

poems.title: Book IX, 13b
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Both are maimed and strolling beggars; but the one has lost the use of his eyes, the other the support of his legs. Each serves the other; for the blind man, taking the lame one on his back, walks gingerly by the aid of eyes not his own. One nature supplied the needs of both; for each contributed to the other his deficiency to form a whole.

poems.title: Book IX, 14
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Phaedo saw an octopus in the shallows by the beach oaring itself along in secret, and seizing it, he threw it rapidly on land before it could twine its eight spirals tightly round his hand. Whirled into a bush it fell on the home of a luckless hare, and twirling round fleet-footed puss’s feet held them bound. The captured was capturer, and you, old man, got the unexpected gift of a booty both from sea and land.

poems.title: Book IX, 29
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Adventure, thou inventor of ships (for thou didst discover the paths of the sea, and didst excite men’s minds by hope of gain), what treacherous timbers didst thou fashion; what lust for gain, oft brought home to them by death, hast thou instilled into men! Of a truth the race of mortals had been a golden one, if the sea, like hell, were viewed from the land in dim distance.

poems.title: Book IX, 34
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: After I had traversed innumerable waves of the limitless sea, and stood firm for a season on the land, I was destroyed not by the sea, the terror of ships, but on shore by fire. Who will say that the sea is the more treacherous of the two? It was the earth on which I came into being that destroyed me, and I lie on the beach, reproaching the land for the fate I expected from the sea.

poems.title: Book IX, 35
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I am the newly-fashioned keel of a ship, and the sea beside which I lay carried me off, raging against me even on land.

poems.title: Book IX, 71
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Overhanging branches of the spreading oak, that from on high shade well men seeking shelter from the untempered heat, leafy boughs roofing closer than tiles, the home of wood-pigeons, the home of cicadas, O noontide branches, guard me, too, who lie beneath your foliage, taking refuge from the rays of the sun.

poems.title: Book IX, 73
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: O alternating flood of the Euboean gulf, vagabond - water, running contrary to thy own current, how strong but inconstant a stream thou lendest to the ships, changing its direction regularly thrice by day and thrice by night! Thou art one of the marvels of life, and I am filled with infinite wonder at thee, but do not seek the reason of thy factious course. It is the business and the secret of Nature.

poems.title: Book IX, 86
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: An omnivorous, crawling, lickerish mouse, seeing in the house an oyster with its lips open, had a bite at its flesh-like wet beard. Immediately the house of shell closed tightly with a clap owing to the pain, and the mouse, locked in the prison from which there was no escape, compassed for himself death and the tomb.

poems.title: Book IX, 156
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Look on the ambush that took Troy after ten years ; look on the horse whose belly was big with the armed and silent Greeks. Epeius is building it and Athena is ordering the work, and all Hellas is emerging from beneath its back. Of a truth in vain did so great a host perish, if stratagem was more helpful to the Atreidae in the war than open battle.

poems.title: Book IX, 178
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I, Rhodes, who once was the Sun’s island, am now Caesar’s, and I boast of equal light from each. Then when I was near extinguished, O Sun, a new ray illuminated me, and Nero’s light shone beside thine. How shall I say to which I owe most? The one brought me to the light from the depths, and the other saved me as I was sinking.

poems.title: Book IX, 192
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: A. “Ye books, who are ye, what do ye contain?” B. “Daughters of Maeonides, and we tell the tales of Troy; one, the wrath of Achilles and the deeds of Hector’s hands, and all the struggles of the ten years’ war; the other, the labours of Ulysses and the tears of good Penelope by her widowed couch.” A. “I worship you and the Muses; for after your song the world could say it possessed eleven Pierian sisters.”

poems.title: Book IX, 222: A Dolphin speaks
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I rook on my back the dripping corpse and bore it to the beach; the beast saved the man, the sea creature that of the land, the living the dead. But what did it avail me? I swam from sea to land, and receive death as payment for my porterage. We interchanged destinies. His land slew me, and my water slew him who belonged to the land.

poems.title: Book IX, 263
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Old Eubule, whenever she had set her heart on anything, used to pick up the nearest stone at her feet, as being Apollo’s prophet, and try it in her hand. Whenever she did not want a thing, it was heavy ; but if she wanted it, it was lighter than a feather. But she acted as it pleased her best, and if she came to grief she set down the unfairness of her hand’s judgment to Phoebus.

poems.title: Book IX, 277
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Way, torrent, in thy furious march dost thou lift thyself up so high and shut off the progress of travellers on foot? Art thou drunk with the rain, and no more content with a stream the Nymphs make transparent? Hast thou borrowed water from the turbid clouds? One day I shall see thee burnt up by the sun, who knows how to test the water of rivers, distinguishing the true from the bastard.

poems.title: Book IX, 294
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: A. “Xerxes gave thee this purple cloak, Leonidas, reverencing thy valorous deeds.” B. “I do not accept it; that is the reward of traitors. Let me be clothed in my shield in death too ; no wealthy funeral forme!” A, “But thou art dead. Why dost thou hate the Persians so bitterly even in death?” B. “The passion for freedom dies not.”

poems.title: Book IX, 298
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: My staff guided me to the temple uninitiated not only in the mysteries, but in the sunlight. The goddesses initiated me into both, and on that night I knew that my eyes as well as my soul had been purged of night. I went back to Athens without a staff, proclaiming the holiness of the mysteries of Demeter more clearly with my eyes than with my tongue.

poems.title: Book IX, 306
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Cease working, ye woodcutters, at least as far as concerns ships. It is no longer pine-trees that glide over the waves but hides. Ships are no longer built with bolts of bronze or iron, but their hulls are held together with flaxen cords, and the same ship now floats on the sea and now travels on land, folded to be mounted on a carriage. Argo was formerly the theme of song, but Pallas has granted to Sabinus to build a still more novel keel.

poems.title: Book IX, 310
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: A little mouse devoured some unfired gold-dust, the scrapings of the file’s iron teeth, lighter than the sands of Libya. It proved a heavy meal for him ; for his belly, trailing with the weight, made the swift creature slow-footed, and so he was caught and cut open, and the stolen treasure extracted from his inside. Even to brutes, gold, thou art the cause of evil.

poems.title: Book IX, 404
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Ah lovely is the liquor of the bees, self-wrought in the ether, and the cells self-moulded and not with hands; a gift unrequited to the life of men, needing no mattock, or oxen, or crooked sickle, but only a little vessel into which the bee pours forth the sweet stream in abundance from its tiny body. Hail! ye pure creatures; pasture on the flowers, ye winged makers of ethereal nectar.

poems.title: Book IX, 413
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: The terebinth island has few vineyards, being small, but is all flat and not rugged. The islands near it are large and broad, but for the most part rough, and superior in this only, their size. We compete for crops, not for furlongs, just as the cornfields of Egypt take no count of the sands of Libya.

poems.title: Book IX, 415: On a Ship built from the Profits of a Brothel
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: I was formerly, too, my master’s partner in his lucrative trade, when the crew he collected consisted of public votaries of Cypris. From those profits he built my keel that Cypris might see me, a product of the land, tossing on the sea. My rig befits a lady of pleasure; I wear dainty white linen, and on my timbers lies a delicate dye. Come, sailors, confidently mount on my stern. I can take any number of oarsmen.

poems.title: Book IX, 546
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Once in a way let my couch be on the ship’s poop, the weather-cloths above sounding with the blows of the spray, the fire breaking out from the stones,’ and the pot upon them bubbling with empty noise. Let my eyes be on the unwashed cabin boy, and let my table be the first plank of the deck that offers; and a game of “‘Give and take” and the gossip of the sailors. The other day this happened to me, who love to be at hail fellow all round.

poems.title: Book IX, 549
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: A. Ye streams of the fountain, why have ye fled? Where is all that water gone? What fiery sun has extinguished the ever-runnng spring? B. We are exhausted by tears for Agricola; his thirsty dust has absorbed all the drink we had to give.

poems.title: Book IX, 551
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Chalcedon hates and punishes the ill-omened heron. Phoebus will tell for what reason it is always called the traitor-bird. When in the shallow sea standing on its thin shanks it was picking up its food from the sand, then the foemen crossed to the city from opposite, learning at length to pass over the sea on foot. Stone the wicked bird, for it got from the enemy a heavy reward—conchs and seaweed, the traitor.

poems.title: Book IX, 242
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Glaucus, brought up on the shores of Thasus, he who conducted those crossing by ferry to the island, skilled ploughman of the sea, who even when he was dozing guided the rudder with no uncertain hand, the old man of countless years, the battered remnant of a seafarer, not even when he was on the point of death quitted his old tub. They burnt his shell on the top of him, that the old man might sail to Hades in his own boat.

poems.title: Book X, 17
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Blest god of the harbour, accompany with gentle breeze the departing sails of Archelaus through the undisturbed water as far as the open sea, and thou who rulest over the extreme point of the beach, save him on his voyage as far as the Pythian shrine. From thence, if all we singers are dear to Phoebus, I will sail trusting in the fair western gale.

poems.title: Book XI, 66
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Even if you smoothen the wrinkled skin of your many-trenched cheeks, and blacken with coal your lidless eyes, and dye your white hair black, and hang round your temples curly ringlets crisped by fire, this is useless and even ridiculous, and even if you go further . . .

poems.title: Book XVI, 136: On the Same
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: When the hand of Timomachus painted baleful Medea, pulled in diverse directions by jealousy and love of her children, he undertook vast labour in trying to draw her two characters, the one inclined to wrath, the other to pity. But he showed both to the full; look at the picture: in her threat dwell tears, and wrath dwells in her pity. The intention is enough, as the sage said. The blood of the children befitted Medea, not the hand of Timomachus.

poems.title: Book XVI, 147: On a Painting of Andromeda
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: The land is Ethiopian; he with the winged sandals is Perseus; she who is chained to the rock is Andromeda; the face is the Gorgon’s, whose glance turns men to stone; the sea-monster is the task set by Love; she who boasted of her child’s beauty is Cassiopea. Andromeda releases from the rock her feet inured to numbness and dead, and her suitor carries off the bride his prize.

poems.title: Book XVI, 333: On Diogenes
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: The wallet and cloak and the barley-dough thickened with water, the staff planted before his feet, and the earthenware cup, are estimated by the wise Dog as sufficient for the needs of life, and even in these there was something superfluous; for, seeing the countryman drinking from the hollow of his hand, he said, “Why, thou earthen cup, did I burden myself with thee to no purpose?”

poems.title: Book XVI, 334: On the Same
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text: Even brass is aged by time, but not all the ages, Diogenes, shall destroy thy fame, since thou alone didst show to mortals the rule of self-sufficiency and the easiest path of life.

poems.title: To the Gods of Harbour and Headland (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Harbour-god, do thou, O blessed one, send with a gentle breeze the outward-bound sail of Archelaus down smooth water even to the sea; and thou who hast the point of the shore in ward, keep the convoy that is bound for the Pythian shrine; and thenceforward, if all we singers are in Phoebus' care, I will sail cheerily on with a fair-flowing west wind.

poems.title: To Artemis of the Ways (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou of the Ways, to thee Antiphilus dedicates this hat from his own head, a voucher of his wayfaring; for thou wast gracious to his prayers, wast favouring to his paths; and his thank-offering is small indeed but sacred. Let not any greedy traveller's hand snatch our gift; sacrilege is not safe even in little things.

poems.title: Under the Oak (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Lofty-hung boughs of the tall oak, a shadowy height over men that take shelter from the fierce heat, fair-foliaged, closer-roofing than tiles, houses of wood-pigeons, houses of crickets, O noontide branches, protect me likewise who lie beneath your tresses, fleeing from the sun's rays.

poems.title: Summer Sailing (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Mine be a mattress on the poop, and the awnings over it surrounding with the blows of the spray, and the fire forcing its way out of the hearth-stones, and a pot upon them with empty turmoil of bubbles; and let me see the boy dressing the meat, and my table be a ship's plank covered with a cloth; and a game of pitch and toss, and the boatswain's whistle: the other day I had such fortune, for I love common life.

poems.title: In Limine Portus (Mackail)
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Already almost in touch of my native land, "To-morrow," I said, "the wind that has set so long against me will abate"; not yet had the speech died on my lip, and the sea was even as Hades, and that light word broke me down. Beware of every speech with to-morrow in it; not even small things escape the Nemesis that avenges the tongue.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.111: εἶπον ἐγὼ καὶ πρόσθεν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
εἶπον ἐγὼ καὶ πρόσθεν, ὅτʼ ἦν ἔτι φίλτρα Τερείνης
νήπια, Συμφλέξει πάντας ἀεξομένη.
οἱ δʼ ἐγέλων τὸν μάντιν. ἴδʼ, ὁ χρόνος ὃν ποτʼ ἐφώνουν,
οὗτος· ἐγὼ δὲ πάλαι τραύματος ᾐσθανόμην.
καὶ τί πάθω; λεύσσειν μέν, ὅλαι φλόγες· ἢν δʼ ἀπονεύσω,
φροντίδες· ἢν δʼ αἰτῶ, παρθένος. οἰχόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca V.307: χεῦμα μὲν Εὐρώταο Δακωνικόν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
χεῦμα μὲν Εὐρώταο Δακωνικόν· ἁ δʼ ἀκάλυπτος
Λήδα· χὠ κύκνῳ κρυπτόμενος Κρονίδας.
οἳ δέ με τὸν δυσέρωτα καταίθετε, καὶ τί γένωμαι
ὄρνεον; εἰ γὰρ Ζεὺς κύκνος, ἐγὼ κόρυδος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.95: Βουστρόφον, ἀκροσίδαρον, ἀπειλητῆρα μύωπα
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Βουστρόφον, ἀκροσίδαρον, ἀπειλητῆρα μύωπα
καὶ πήραν μέτρον σιτοδόκον σπορίμου,
γαμψόν τε δρέπανον σταχυητόμον, ὅπλον ἀρούρης,
καὶ παλινουροφόρον, χεῖρα θέρευς τρίνακα,
καὶ τρητοὺς ποδεῶνας ὁ γατόμος ἄνθετο Δηοῖ
Πάρμις, ἀνιηρῶν παυσάμενος καμάτων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.97: Δοῦρας Ἀλεξάνδροιο· λέγει δέ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Δοῦρας Ἀλεξάνδροιο· λέγει δέ σε γράμματʼ ἐκεῖνον
ἐκ πολέμου θέσθαι σύμβολον Ἀρτέμιδι
ὅπλον ἀνικήτοιο βραχίονος. ἆ καλὸν ἔγχος,
ᾧ πόντος καὶ χθὼν εἶκε κραδαινομένῳ.
ἵλαθι, δοῦρας ἀταρβές· ἀεὶ δέ σε πᾶς τις ἀθρήσας
ταρβήσει, μεγάλης μνησάμενος παλάμης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.199: Εἰνοδίη, σοὶ τόνδε φίλης
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Εἰνοδίη, σοὶ τόνδε φίλης ἀνεθήκατο κόρσης
πῖλον, ὁδοιπορίης σύμβολον, Ἀντίφιλος·
ἦσθα γὰρ εὐχωλῇσι κατήκοος, ἦσθα κελεύθοις
ἵλαος· οὐ πολλὴ δʼ ἡ χάρις, ἀλλʼ ὁσίη.
μὴ δέ τις ἡμετέρου μάρψῃ χερὶ μάργος ὁδίτης
ἀνθέματος· συλᾶν ἀσφαλὲς οὐδʼ ὀλίγα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.250: λιτὸς ἐγὼ τὰ τύχης
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
λιτὸς ἐγὼ τὰ τύχης, ὦ δεσπότι· φημὶ δὲ πολλῶν
ὄλβον ὑπερκύπτειν τὸν σὸν ἀπὸ κραδίης.
ἀλλὰ δέχευ μνιαροῖο βαθυρρήνοιο τάπητος
ἐνδυτὸν εὐανθεῖ πορφύρῃ εἰδόμενον,
εἴριά τε ῥοδόεντα, καὶ ἐς κυανότριχα χαίτην
νάρδον, ὑπὸ γλαυκῆς κλειομένην ὑάλου,
ὄφρα χιτὼν μὲν χρῶτα περισκέπῃ, ἔργα δʼ ἐλέγχῃ
χεῖρας, ὁ δʼ εὐώδης ἀτμὸς ἔχῃ πλοκάμους.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.252: μῆλον ἐγὼ στρούθειον ἀπὸ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
μῆλον ἐγὼ στρούθειον ἀπὸ προτέρης ἔτι ποίης
ὥριον ἐν νεαρῷ χρωτὶ φυλασσόμενον,
ἄσπιλον, ἀρρυτίδωτον, ἰσόχνοον ἀρτιγόνοισιν,
ἀκμὴν εὐπετάλοις συμφυὲς ἀκρεμόσιν,
ὥρης χειμερίης σπάνιον γέρας; εἰς σὲ δʼ, ἄνασσα,
τοίην χὠ νιφόεις κρυμὸς ὀπωροφορεῖ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VI.257: τίς με, Διωνύσῳ πεπλασμένον
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
τίς με, Διωνύσῳ πεπλασμένον ἀμφιφορῆα,
τίς με, τὸν Ἀδριακοῦ νέκταρος οἰνοδόκον,
Δηοῦς ἐπλήρωσε; τίς ὁ φθόνος εἰς ἐμὲ Βάκχου,
ἢ σπάνις οἰκείου τεύχεος ἀσταχύων;
ἀμφοτέρους ᾔσχυνε· σεσύληται μὲν ὁ Βάκχος,
Δημήτηρ δὲ Μέθην σύντροφον οὐ δέχεται,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.141: Θεσσαλὲ Πρωτεσίλαε, σὲ μὲν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Θεσσαλὲ Πρωτεσίλαε, σὲ μὲν πολὺς ᾅσεται αἰὼν,
Τροίᾳ ὀφειλομένου πτώματος ἀρξάμενου·
σῆμα δέ τοι πτελέῃσι συνηρεφὲς ἀμφικομεῦσι
νύμφαι, ἀπεχθομένης Ἰλίου ἀντιπέρας·
δένδρα δὲ δυσμήνιτα, καὶ ἢν ποτὶ τεῖχος ἴδωσι
Τρώιον, αὐαλέαν φυχλλοχοεῦντι κόμην,
ὅσσος ἐν ἡρώεσσι τότʼ ἦν χόλος, εἰ μέρος ἀκμὴν
ἐχθρὸν ἐν ἀψύχοις σώζεται ἀκρεμόσιν ;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.175: οὕτω πᾶσ’ ἀπόλωλε, γεωπόνε
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
οὕτω πᾶσ’ ἀπόλωλε, γεωπόνε, βῶλος ἀρότροις,
ἤδη καὶ τύμβους νωτοβατοῦσι βόες,
ἡ δʼ ὕνις ἐν νεκύεσσι; τί τοι πλέον; ἢ πόσος οὗτος
πυρός, ὃν ἐκ τέφρης, κοὐ χθονὸς ἁρπάσετε;
οὐκ αἰεὶ ζήσεσθε, καὶ ὑμέας ἄλλος ἀρώσει,
τοίης ἀρξαμένους πᾶσι κακοσπορίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.176: οὐχ ὅτι με φθίμενον
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
οὐχ ὅτι με φθίμενον κῆδος λίπεν, ἐνθάδε κεῖμαι
γυμνὸς ὑπὲρ γαίης πυροφόροιο νέκυς·
ταρχύθην γὰρ ἐγὼ τὸ πρίν ποτε, νῦν δʼ ἀροτῆρος
χερσὶ σιδηρείη μʼ ἐξεκύλισεν ὕνις.
ἦ ῥα κακῶν θάνατόν τις ἐρεῖ λύσιν, ὁππότʼ ἐμεῖο,
ξεῖνε, πέλει παθέων ὕστατον οὐδὲ τάφος;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.375: δώματά μοι σεισθέντα κατήριπεν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
δώματά μοι σεισθέντα κατήριπεν· ἀλλʼ ἐμὸς ἀπτὼς
ἦν θάλαμος, τοίχων ὀρθὰ τιναξαμένων,
οἷς ὑποφωλεύουσαν ὑπήλυθον αἱ κακόμοιροι
ὠδῖνες· σεισμῷ δʼ ἄλλον ἔμιξα φόβον.
μαῖα δέ μοι λοχίων αὐτὴ φύσις· ἀμφότεροι δὲ
κοινὸν ὑπὲρ γαίης εἴδομεν ἠέλιον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.379: α. εἰπέ, Δικαιάρχεια, τί
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.399: τηλοτάτω χεύασθαι ἔδει τάφον
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
τηλοτάτω χεύασθαι ἔδει τάφον Οἰδιπόδαο
παισὶν ἀπʼ ἀλλήλων, οἷς πέρας οὐδʼ Ἀίδας·
ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς Ἀχέροντος ἕνα πλόον ἠρνήσαντο,
χὠ στυγερὸς ζώει κἠν φθιμένοισιν Ἄρης.
ἠνίδε πυρκαϊῆς ἄνισον φλόγα· δαιομένα γὰρ
ἐξ ἑνὸς εἰς δισσὰν δῆριν ἀποστρέφεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.622: Βόρχος ὁ βουποίμην ὅτʼ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Βόρχος ὁ βουποίμην ὅτʼ ἐπὶ γλυκὺ κηρίον εἷρπεν,
αἰγίλιπα σχοίνῳ πέτρον ἐπερχόμενος,
εἵπετό οἱ σκυλάκων τις ὁ καὶ βοσίν, ὃς φάγε λεπτὴν
σχοῖνον ἀνελκομένῳ χραινομένην μέλιτι·
κάππεσε δʼ εἰς Ἀίδαο· τὸ δʼ ἀτρυγὲς ἀνδράσιν ἄλλοις
κεῖνο μέλι ψυχῆς ὤνιον εἰρύσατο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.630: ἤδη που πάτρης πελάσας
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἤδη που πάτρης πελάσας σχεδόν, αὔριον, εἶπον,
ἡ μακρὴ κατʼ ἐμοῦ δυσπλοΐη κοπάσει.
οὔπω χεῖλος ἔμυσε, καὶ ἦν ἴσος Ἄϊδι πόντος,
καί με κατέτρυχεν κεῖνο τὸ κοῦφον ἔπος.
πάντα λόγον πεφύλαξο τὸν αὔριον· οὐδὲ τὰ μικρὰ
λήθει τὴν γλώσσης ἀντίπαλον Νέμεσιν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.634: Νεκροδόκον κλιντῆρα Φίλων ὁ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Νεκροδόκον κλιντῆρα Φίλων ὁ πρέσβυς ἀείρων
ἐγκλιδόν, ὄφρα λάβοι μισθὸν ἐφημέριον,
σφάλματος ἐξ ὀλίγοιο πεσὼν θάνεν ἦν γὰρ ἕτοιμος
εἰς ἀίδην, ἐκάλει δʼ ἡ πολιὴ πρόφασιν
ὃν δʼ ἄλλοις ἐφόρει νεκυοστόλον, αὐτὸς ἐφʼ αὑτῷ
ἀσκάντην ὁ γέρων ἀχθοφορῶν ἔλαθεν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.635: ναῦν Ἱεροκλείδης ἔσχεν σύγγηρον
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ναῦν Ἱεροκλείδης ἔσχεν σύγγηρον, ὁμόπλουν,
τὴν αὐτὴν ζωῆς καὶ θανάτου σύνοδον,
πιστὴν ἰχθυβολεῦντι συνέμπορον. οὔτις ἐκείνης
πώποτʼ ἐπέπλωσεν κῦμα δικαιοτέρη·
γήραος ἄχρις ἔβοσκε πονευμένη· εἶτα θανόντα
ἐκτέρισεν· συνέπλω δʼ ἄχρι καὶ Ἀίδεω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca VII.641: σῆμα δυωδεκάμοιρον ἀφεγγέος ἠελίοιο
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
σῆμα δυωδεκάμοιρον ἀφεγγέος ἠελίοιο,
τοσσάκις ἀγλώσσῳ φθεγγόμενον στόματι,
εὖτʼ ἂν θλιβομένοιο ποτὶ στενὸν ὕδατος ἀὴρ
αὐλὸν ἀποστείλῃ πνεῦμα διωλύγιον,
θῆκεν Ἀθήναιος δήμῳ χάριν, ὡς ἂν ἐναργὴς
εἴη κἠν φθονεραῖς ἠέλιος νεφέλαις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.13b: ἄμφω μὲν πηροὶ καὶ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἄμφω μὲν πηροὶ καὶ ἀλήμονες, ἀλλʼ ὁ μὲν ὄψεις,
ὃς δὲ βάσεις· ἄλλου δʼ ἄλλος ὑπηρεσίη·
τυφλὸς γὰρ χωλοῖο κατωμάδιον βάρος αἴρων
ἀτραπὸν ὀθνείοις ὄμμασιν ἀκροβάτει.
ἡ μία δʼ ἀμφοτέροις ἤρκει φύσις· ἐν γὰρ ἑκάστῳ
τοὐλλιπὲς ἀλλήλοις εἰς ὅλον ἠράνισαν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.14: αἰγιαλοῦ τενάγεσσιν ὑποπλώοντα λαθραίῃ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
αἰγιαλοῦ τενάγεσσιν ὑποπλώοντα λαθραίῃ
εἰρεσίῃ Φαίδων εἴσιδε πουλυπόδην
μάρψας δʼ ὠκὺς ἔριψεν ἐπὶ χθόνα, πρὶν περὶ χεῖρας
πλέξασθαι βρύγδην ὀκτατόνους ἕλικας·
δισκευθεὶς δʼ ἐπὶ θάμνον ἐς οἰκία δειλὰ λαγωοῦ,
εἰληδὸν ταχινοῦ πτωκὸς ἔδησε πόδας·
εἷλε δʼ ἁλούς· σὺ δʼ ἄελπτον ἔχεις γέρας ἀμφοτέρωθεν
ἄγρης χερσαίης, πρέσβυ, καὶ εἰναλίης,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.29: τόλμα, νεῶν ἀρχηγὲ ʽσὺ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
τόλμα, νεῶν ἀρχηγὲ ʽσὺ γὰρ δρόμον ηὕραο πόντου,
καὶ ψυχὰς ἀνδρῶν κέρδεσιν ἠρέθισασʼ,
οἷον ἐτεκτήνω δόλιον ξύλον, οἷον ἐνῆκας
ἀνθρώποις θανάτῳ κέρδος ἐλεγχόμενον;
ἦν ὄντως μερόπων χρύσεον γένος, εἰ γʼ ἀπὸ χέρσου
τηλόθεν, ὡς Ἀίδης, πόντος ἀπεβλέπετο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.34: μυρία με τρίψασαν ἀμετρήτοιο
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
μυρία με τρίψασαν ἀμετρήτοιο θαλάσσης
κύματα, καὶ χέρσῳ βαιὸν ἐρεισαμένην,
ὤλεσεν οὐχὶ θάλασσα, νεῶν φόβος, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ γαίης
Ἥφαιστος. τίς ἐρεῖ πόντον ἀπιστότερον;
ἔνθεν ἔφυν ἀπόλωλα· παρʼ ἠιόνεσσι δὲ κεῖμαι,
χέρσῳ τὴν πελάγευς ἐλπίδα μεμφομένη.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.35: ἄρτι με πηγνυμένην ἀκάτου
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἄρτι με πηγνυμένην ἀκάτου τρόπιν ἔσπασε γείτων
πόντος, κἠν χέρσῳ εἰς ἐμὲ μηνάμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.71: κλῶνες ἀπῃόριοι ταναῆς δρυός
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
κλῶνες ἀπῃόριοι ταναῆς δρυός, εὔσκιον ὕψος
ἀνδράσιν ἄκρητον καῦμα φυλασσομένοις,
εὐπέταλοι, κεράμων στεγανώτεροι, οἰκία φαττῶν,
οἰκία τεττίγων, ἔνδιοι ἀκρεμόνες,
κἠμὲ τὸν ὑμετέραισιν ὑποκλινθέντα κόμαισιν
ῥύσασθʼ, ἀκτίνων ἠελίου φυγάδα,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.73: Εὐβοϊκοῦ κόλποιο παλινδίνητε θάλασσα
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Εὐβοϊκοῦ κόλποιο παλινδίνητε θάλασσα,
πλαγκτὸν ὕδωρ, ἰδίοις ῥεύμασιν ἀντίπαλον,
ἠελίῳ κἠν νυκτὶ τεταγμένον ἐς τρίς, ἄπιστον
ναυσὶν ὅσον πέμπεις χεῦμα δανειζόμενον
θαῦμα βίου, θαμβῶ σε τὸ μυρίον, οὑ δὲ ματεύω
σὴν στάσιν ἀρρήτῳ ταῦτα μέμηλε φύσει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.86: Παμφάγος ἑρπηστὴς κατὰ δώματα
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Παμφάγος ἑρπηστὴς κατὰ δώματα λιχνοβόρος μῦς,
ὄστρεον ἀθρήσας χείλεσι πεπταμένον,
πώγωνος διεροῖο νόθην ὠδάξατο σάρκα
αὐτίκα δʼ ὀστρακόεις ἐπλατάγησε δόμος,
ἁρμόσθη δʼ ὀδύναισιν ὁ δʼ ἐν κλείθροισιν ἀφύκτοις
ληφθεὶς αὐτοφόνον τύμβον ἐπεσπάσατο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.156: Δέρκεο τὸν Τροίας
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Δέρκεο τὸν Τροίας δεκέτη λόχον εἴσιδε πῶλον
εὐόπλου Δαναῶν ἔγκυον ἡσυχίης.
τεκταίνει μὲν Ἐπειός, Ἀθηναίη δὲ κελεύει
ἔργον· ὑπὲκ νώτου δʼ Ἑλλὰς ὅλα δύεται.
ἦ ῥα μάταν ἀπόλοντο τόσος στρατός, εἰ πρὸς Ἄρηα
ἦν δόλος Ἀτρείδαις ἐσθλότερος πολέμου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.178: ὡς πάρος Ἀελίου, νῦν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ὡς πάρος Ἀελίου, νῦν Καίσαρος ἁ Ῥόδος εἰμὶ
νᾶσος, ἴσον δʼ αὐχῶ φέγγος ἀπʼ ἀμφοτέρων.
ἤδη σβεννυμέναν με νέα κατεφώτισεν ἀκτίς,
Ἅλιε, καὶ παρὰ σὸν φέγγος ἔλαμψε Νέρων.
πῶς εἴπω τίνι μᾶλλον ὀφείλομαι; ὃς μὲν ἔδειξεν
ἐξ ἁλός, ὃς δʼ ἤδη ῥύσατο δυομέναν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.192: α. αἱ βίβλοι, τίνες
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
α. αἱ βίβλοι, τίνες ἐστέ; τί κεύθετε; β. θυγατέρες μὲν
Μαιονίδου, μύθων δʼ ἵστορες Ἰλιακῶν
ἁ μία μὲν μηνιθμὸν Ἀχιλλέος, ἔργα τε χειρὸς
Ἑκτορέας, δεκέτους τʼ ἆθλα λέγει πολέμου·
ἁ δʼ ἑτέρα μόχθον τὸν
Ὀδυσσέος, ἀμφί τε λέκτροις
χηρείοις ἀγαθᾶς δάκρυα Πηνελόπας.
α. Ἵλατε σὺν Μούσαισι· μεθʼ ὑμετέρας γὰρ ἀοιδὰς
εἶπεν ἔχειν αἰὼν ἕνδεκα Πιερίδας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.222: ἀνέρα θήρ, χερσαῖον ὁ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἀνέρα θήρ, χερσαῖον ὁ πόντιος, ἄπνοον ἔμπνους,
ἀράμενος λοφιῆς ὑγρὸν ὕπερθε νέκυν,
εἰς ψαμάθους ἐκόμισσα. τί δὲ πλέον; ἐξ ἁλὸς εἰς γῆν
νηξάμενος, φόρτου μισθὸν ἔχω θάνατον
δαίμονα δʼ ἀλλήλων ἠμείψαμεν ἡ μὲν ἐκείνου
χθὼν ἐμέ, τὸν δʼ ἀπὸ γῆς ἔκτανε τοὐμὸν ὕδωρ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.242: Γλαῦκος ὁ νησαίοιο διαπλώουσιν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Γλαῦκος ὁ νησαίοιο διαπλώουσιν ὁδηγὸς
πορθμοῦ, καὶ Θασίων ἔντροφος αἰγιαλῶν,
πόντου ἀροτρευτὴρ ἐπιδέξιος, οὐδʼ, ὅτʼ ἔκνωσσεν,
πλαζομένῃ στρωφῶν πηδάλιον παλάμῃ,
μυριέτης, ἁλίοιο βίου ῥάκος, οὐδʼ, ὅτʼ ἔμελλεν
θνῄσκειν, ἐκτὸς ἔβη γηραλέης σανίδος·
τοὶ δὲ κέλυφος ἔκαυσαν ἐπʼ ἀνέρι, τόφρʼ ὁ γεραιὸς
πλώσῃ ἐπʼ οἰκείης εἰς ἀίδην ἀκάτου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.263: ἡ γραῦς Εὐβούλη, ὅτε
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἡ γραῦς Εὐβούλη, ὅτε οἱ καταθύμιον ἦν τι,
Φοίβου τὸν πρὸ ποδῶν μάντιν ἄειρε λίθον,
χείρεσι πειράζουσα· καὶ ἦν βαρύς, ἡνίκα μή τι
ἤθελεν εἰ δὲ θέλοι, κουφότερος πετάλων.
αὐτὴ δὲ πρήσσουσα τὸ οἱ φίλον, ἤν ποθʼ ἁμάρτῃ,
Φοίβῳ τὰς ἀνίσους χεῖρας ἐπεγράφετο.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.277: Λαβροπόδη χείμαρρε, τί δὴ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Λαβροπόδη χείμαρρε, τί δὴ τόσον ὧδε κορύσσῃ,
πεζὸν ἀποκλείων ἴχνος ὁδοιπορίης;
ἦ μεθύεις ὄμβροισι, καὶ οὐ Νύμφαισι διαυγὲς
νᾶμα φέρεις, θολεραῖς δʼ ἠράνισαι νεφέλαις.
ὄψομαι ἠελίῳ σε κεκαυμένον, ὅστις ἐλέγχειν
καὶ γόνιμον ποταμῶν καὶ νόθον οἶδεν ὕδωρ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.294: α. πορφυρέαν τοι τάνδε
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
α. πορφυρέαν τοι τάνδε, Λεωνίδα, ὤπασε χλαῖναν
Ξέρξης, ταρβήσας ἔργα τεᾶς ἀρετᾶς.
β. οὐ δέχομαι· προδόταις αὕτα χάρις. ἀσπὶς ἔχοι με
καὶ νέκυν ὁ πλοῦτος δʼ οὐκ ἐμὸν ἐντάφιον.
α. ἀλλʼ ἔθανες· τί τοσόνδε καὶ ἐν νεκύεσσιν ἀπεχθὴς
Πέρσαις; β. οὐ θνᾴσκει ζᾶλος ἐλευθερίας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.298: Σκίπων με πρὸς νηὸν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Σκίπων με πρὸς νηὸν ἀνήγαγεν, ὄντα βέβηλον
οὐ μοῦνον τελετῆς, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἠελίου·
μύστην δʼ ἀμφοτέρων με Θεαὶ θέσαν οἶδα δʼ ἐκείνῃ
νυκτὶ καὶ ὀφθαλμῶν νύκτα καθηράμενος.
ἀσκίπων δʼ εἰς ἄστυ κατέστιχον, ὄργια Δηοῦς
κηρύσσων γλώσσης ὄμμασι τρανότερον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.306: ὑλοτόμοι παύσασθε, νεῶν χάριν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ὑλοτόμοι παύσασθε, νεῶν χάριν. οὐκέτι πεύκη
κύματος, ἀλλʼ ἤδη ῥινὸς ἐπιτροχάει·
γόμφος δʼ οὐδʼ ἔτι χαλκὸς ἐν ὁλκάσιν, οὐδὲ σίδηρος,
ἀλλὰ λίνῳ τοίχων ἁρμονίη δέδεται.
τὰς δʼ αὐτὰς ποτὲ πόντος ἔχει νέας, ἄλλοτε γαῖα
πτυκτὸν ἀμαξίτην φόρτον ἀειρομένας.
Ἀργὼ μὲν προτέροισιν ἀοίδιμος· ἀλλὰ Σαβίνῳ
καινοτέρην πῆξαι Παλλὰς ἔνευσε τρόπιν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.310: Ψῆγμʼ ἄπυρον χρυσοῖο σιδηρείων
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Ψῆγμʼ ἄπυρον χρυσοῖο σιδηρείων ὑπʼ ὀδόντων
ῥινηθέν, Λιβυκῆς κουφότερον ψαμάθου,
μῦς ὀλίγος βαρὺ δεῖπνον ἐδαίσατο· πᾶσα δὲ νηδὺς
συρομένη βραδύπουν θῆκε τὸν ὠκύτατον.
ληφθεὶς δʼ ἐκ μεσάτης ἀνετέμνετο κλέμματα γαστρός·
ἦς ἄρα κἠν ἀλόγοις, χρυσέ, κακοῦ πρόφασις,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.404: ἆ καλὸν αὐτοπόνητον ἐν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἆ καλὸν αὐτοπόνητον ἐν αἰθέρι ῥεῦμα μελισσῶν,
κἄπλαστοι χειρῶν αὐτοπαγεῖς θαλάμαι,
προίκιος ἀνθρώπων βιότῳ χάρις, οὐχὶ μακέλλας,
οὐ βοός, οὐ γαμψῶν δευομένα δρεπάνων,
γαυλοῦ δὲ σμικροῖο, τόθι γλυκὺ νᾶμα μέλισσα
πηγάζει σκήνευς δαψιλὲς ἐξ ὀλίγου.
χαίροιτʼ εὐαγέες, καὶ ἐν ἄνθεσι ποιμαίνεσθε,
αἰθερίου πτηναὶ νέκταρος ἐργάτιδες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.413: ἡ τερεβινθώδης ὀλιγάμπελος οἷά
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἡ τερεβινθώδης ὀλιγάμπελος οἷά τε βαιὴ
νησίς, ἀλλʼ ὁμαλὴ πᾶσα καὶ ἀστύφελος·
αἱ δʼ ἀγχοῦ, μεγάλαι τε καὶ εὐρέες, ἀλλʼ ἐπὶ πουλὺ
τρηχεῖαι· μεγέθει τοῦτο περισσότεραι.
καρποῖς, οὐ σταδίοισιν ἐρίζομεν οὐδὲ γὰρ αὖλαξ
Αἰγύπτου Λιβύης ψάμμου ἐπιστρέφεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.415: ἤμην καὶ προπάροιθε συνέμπορος
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἤμην καὶ προπάροιθε συνέμπορος ἀνέρι κέρδους,
ἡνίκα δημοτέρην Κύπριν ἐναυτολόγει·
κεῖθεν καὶ συνέπηξεν ἐμὴν τρόπιν, ὄφρα με λεύσσῃ
Κύπρις, τὴν ἀπὸ γῆς εἰν ἁλὶ ῥεμβομένην.
ἔστιν ἑταίρειος μὲν ἐμοὶ στόλος, εἰσὶ δὲ λεπτὰ
κάρπασα, καὶ λεπτὸν φῦκος ὑπὲρ σανίδων.
ναυτίλοι, ἀλλʼ ἄγε πάντες ἐμῆς ἐπιβαίνετε πρύμνης
θαρραλέως· πολλοὺς οἶδα φέρειν ἐρέτας.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.546: κἠν πρύμνῃ λαχέτω μέ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
κἠν πρύμνῃ λαχέτω μέ ποτε στιβάς, αἳ θʼ ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς
ἠχεῦσαι ψακάδων τύμματι διφθερίδες,
καὶ πῦρ ἐκ μυλάκων βεβιημένον, ἥ τʼ ἐπὶ τούτων
χύτρη, καὶ κενεὸς πομφολύγων θόρυβος,
καί κε ῥυπῶντʼ ἐσίδοιμι διήκονον ἡ δὲ τράπεζα
ἔστω μοι στρωτὴ νηὸς ὕπερθε σανίς·
δὸς λάβε, καὶ ψιθύρισμα τὸ ναυτικόν· εἶχε τύχη τις
πρῴην τοιαύτη τὸν φιλόκοινον ἐμέ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.549: α. κρηναῖαι λιβάδες, τί
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca IX.551: Καλχαδὼν δύστηνον ἐρωδιὸν ἐχθρὰ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Καλχαδὼν δύστηνον ἐρωδιὸν ἐχθρὰ κολάζει·
τεῦ χάριν ὁ προδότης ὄρνις ἀεὶ λέγεται,
† Φοῖβοσἐρεῖ· τεναγῖτιν ὅτʼ εἰς ἅλα κῶλον ἐλαφρὸν
στήσας, ψαμμίτην δόρπον [ ἐθημολόγει,
δυσμενέες τότʼ ἔβησαν ἐπὶ πτόλιν ἀντιπέρηθεν,
ὀψὲ διδασκόμενοι πεζοβατεῖν πέλαγος.
βάλλετε δὴ κακὸν ὄρνιν, ἐπεὶ βαρὺν ἤρατο μισθὸν
ἐκ δηίων, κόχλους καὶ βρύον, ὁ προδότης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca X.17: Ἀρχέλεω, λιμενῖτα, σὺ μέν
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Ἀρχέλεω, λιμενῖτα, σὺ μέν, μάκαρ, ἠπίῳ αὔρῃ
πέμπε κατὰ σταθερῆς οἰχομένην; ὀθόνην
ἄχρις ἐπὶ Τρίτωνα· σὺ δʼ ἠόνος ἄκρα λελογχὼς
τὴν ἐπὶ Πυθείου ῥύεο ναυστολίην·
κεῖθεν δʼ, εἰ Φοίβῳ μεμελήμεθα πάντες ἀοιδοί,
πλεύσομαι εὐαεῖ θαρσαλέως ζεφύρῳ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.66: κἢν τείνῃς ῥακόεντα πολυτμήτοιο
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
κἢν τείνῃς ῥακόεντα πολυτμήτοιο παρειῆς
χρῶτα, καὶ ἀβλεφάρους ὦπας ἐπανθρακίσῃς,
καὶ λευκὴν βάψῃς μέλανι τρίχα, καὶ πυρίφλεκτα
βοστρύχια κροτάφοις οὖλα περικρεμάσῃς,
οὐδὲν ταῦτα, γελοῖα, καὶ ἢν ἔτι πλείονα ῥέξῃς,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.136: τὰν ὀλοὰν Μήδειαν ὅτʼ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
τὰν ὀλοὰν Μήδειαν ὅτʼ ἔγραφε Τιμομάχου χείρ,
ζάλῳ καὶ τέκνοις ἀντιμεθελκομέναν,
μυρίον ἄρατο μόχθον, ἵνʼ ἤθεα δισσὰ χαράξῃ,
ὧν τὸ μὲν εἰς ὀργὰν νεῦε, τὸ δʼ εἰς ἔλεον.
ἄμφω δʼ ἐπλήρωσεν· ὅρα τύπον ἐν γάρ ἀπειλᾷ
δάκρυον, ἐν δʼ ἐλέῳ θυμὸς ἀναστρέφεται.
ἀρκεῖ δʼ ἁ μέλλησις, ἔφα σοφός· αἷμα δὲ τέκνων
ἔπρεπε Μηδείῃ, κοὐ χερὶ Τιμομάχου.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.147: Αἰθιόπων ἁ βῶλος· ὁ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
Αἰθιόπων ἁ βῶλος· ὁ δὲ πτερόεις τὰ πέδιλα,
Περσεύς· ἁ δὲ λίθῳ πρόσδετος Ἀνδρομέδα·
ἁ προτομὰ Γοργοῦς λιθοδερκέος· ἆθλον ἔρωτος,
κῆτος· Κασσιόπας ἁ λάλος εὐτεκνία·
χἁ μὲν ἀπὸ σκοπέλοιο χαλᾷ πόδας ἠθάδι νάρκᾳ
νωθρούς· χὡ μναστὴρ νυμφοκομεῖ τὸ γέρας

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.333: ἡ πήρη καὶ χλαῖνα
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
ἡ πήρη καὶ χλαῖνα καὶ ὕδατι πιληθεῖσα
μάζα, καὶ ἡ πρὸ ποδῶν ῥάβδος ἐρειδομένη,
καὶ δέπας ἐκ κεράμοιο, σοφῷ κυνὶ μέτρα βίοιο
ἄρκια κἠν τούτοις ἦν τι περισσότερον
κοίλαις γὰρ πόμα χερσὶν ἰδὼν ἀρύοντα βοώτην,
εἶπε· τί καὶ σὲ μάτην, ὄστρακον, ἠχθοφόρουν;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XVI.334: γηράσκει καὶ χαλκὸς ὑπὸ
poems.author: Antiphilus of Byzantium
poems.text:
γηράσκει καὶ χαλκὸς ὑπὸ χρόνου· ἀλλὰ σὸν οὔτι
κῦδος ὁ πᾶς αἰών, Διόγενες, καθελεῖ·
μοῦνος ἐπεὶ βιοτᾶς αὐτάρκεα δόξαν ἔδειξας
θνητοῖς, καὶ ζωῆς οἶμον ἐλαφροτάτην.
